title: Informal Conjecture (f(n) = 2n−2)
statement_text: We suspect that Segal-Halevi's construction showing $f(n)\ge 2n-2$ reflects the truth and that $f(n) = 2n - 2$ for all $n \geq 2$.
context_text: In this cake-cutting setting the cake is $[0,1]$ and $n\ge2$ agents have non-atomic Borel probability measures $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ on it. Given non-negative demands $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ summing to $1$, a disproportionate division is a partition $X_1\cup\dots\cup X_n$ of $[0,1]$ with $\mu_i(X_i)\ge\alpha_i$ for all $i$, and $f(n)$ is the maximum, over all measures and demands, of the minimum number of cuts (points splitting $[0,1]$ into intervals that are then distributed) needed for a disproportionate division with $n$ agents. For equal demands $1/n$, $n-1$ cuts suffice and are necessary. Folklore arguments based on the Stromquist–Woodall theorem give $O(n^2)$ cuts, and Segal-Halevi gave $O(n\log n)$; the authors prove $f(n)\le3n-4$ for all $n\ge2$ by a constructive combinatorial argument. Segal-Halevi's lower-bound construction takes $\mu_1$ uniform on $[0,1]$ and, for $1\le i\le n-1$, $\mu_{i+1}$ uniform on a tiny interval around $i/n$, with demand nearly $1$ for agent 1 and tiny equal demands for the others: any disproportionate division needs two cuts in the support of each of $\mu_2,\dots,\mu_n$, hence $f(n)\ge2n-2$. The authors believe deeper topological considerations drive the conjecture: they propose a measure-partitioning conjecture on the circle (for $n$ non-atomic probability measures on $S^1$ and demands summing to $1$, there are a partition $[n]=P\cup Q$ into nonempty sets and a partition of $S^1$ into two intervals $X,X^c$ with $\min_{i\in P}\mu_i(X)=\sum_{j\in P}\alpha_j$ and $\min_{i\in Q}\mu_i(X^c)=\sum_{j\in Q}\alpha_j$) which would imply $f(n)=2n-2$ by a simple induction. This is a measure-partitioning problem rather than a graph problem.

title: Conjecture 3.1
statement_text: For any $n \geq 2$ non-atomic probability measures $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_n$ on the unit circle $S^1$ and non-negative reals $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ summing to $1$, there exists a partition of the set $[n] = P \cup Q$ into two nonempty sets and a partition of the circle $S^1 = X \cup X^c$ into two intervals such that $$\min_{i \in P} \mu_i(X) = \sum_{j \in P} \alpha_j \quad \text{and} \quad \min_{i \in Q} \mu_i(X^c) = \sum_{j \in Q} \alpha_j.$$
context_text: In this cake-cutting setting the cake is $[0,1]$ and $n\ge2$ agents have non-atomic Borel probability measures $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ on it. Given non-negative demands $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ summing to $1$, a disproportionate division is a partition $X_1\cup\dots\cup X_n$ of $[0,1]$ with $\mu_i(X_i)\ge\alpha_i$ for all $i$, and $f(n)$ is the maximum, over all measures and demands, of the minimum number of cuts (points splitting $[0,1]$ into intervals that are then distributed) needed for a disproportionate division with $n$ agents. For equal demands $1/n$, $n-1$ cuts suffice and are necessary. Folklore arguments based on the Stromquist–Woodall theorem give $O(n^2)$ cuts, and Segal-Halevi gave $O(n\log n)$; the authors prove $f(n)\le3n-4$ for all $n\ge2$ by a constructive combinatorial argument. Segal-Halevi's construction shows $f(n)\ge2n-2$, and the authors suspect $f(n)=2n-2$. They propose this measure-partitioning conjecture as the topological statement behind it: if true, a simple inductive argument would give $f(n)=2n-2$ for all $n\ge2$, which would be optimal. Here an interval of the circle is a connected arc, and $X^c$ is the complementary arc. The case of two measures is known and is essentially the Stromquist–Woodall theorem, but the authors were unable to decide the conjecture even for three measures. This is a measure-partitioning problem rather than a graph problem.
